newsitem.title: UK: Europe pays tribute to Kohl's long-service record.
newsitem.headline: Europe pays tribute to Kohl's long-service record.

text.p: European leaders and commentators paid tribute to Helmut Kohl, who overtakes Konrad Adenauer on Thursday as Germany's longest-serving post-war chancellor, but some put his success down to doggedness more than sophistication.
France's left-wing daily Liberation declared in a headline: "Helmut Kohl, the colossus of Europe" and the conservative daily Le Figaro praised the centre-right politician in an editorial.
"He reunited Germany in less time than it takes to write (the word)," it said.
Adenauer, founding father of the West German state, was in office for 14 years and one month from 1949 to 1963 though his political powers, unlike Kohl's, seemed to wane in later years.
Commentators and politicians singled out German unification as Kohl's greatest achievement and praised him as one of the chief driving forces behind European integration.
"Of all the qualities attributed to him, perhaps his perseverance, or if you prefer, obstinacy, is the one which has served him best," Italian daily Corriere della Sera said.

"He isn't an intellectual but his simple and strong ideas have spoken to the hearts of millions of people; his vocabulary lacking in refinement has enabled ordinary Germans to identify totally with him," it said.

La Stampa devoted a whole page to Kohl's anniversary under the headline "The grey helmsman who dared to dream", adding that in a few more years Kohl, now 66, could break the 19-year record of Germany's "Iron Chancellor" Otto von Bismarck last century.

While acknowledging his meteoric rise from humble origins to become a top-ranking world leader, some gently mocked Kohl, who has been dubbed "Bismarck in a cardigan", and his only self-confessed passion apart from politics -- food.

"There is something reassuring about a powerful German chancellor who, when he wakes up in the middle of the night, is thinking by his own admission about raiding the refrigerator, not re-arranging the world," Britain's Economist said.
"Helmut Kohl is a leader who at first looked cloddishly ordinary and has grown extraordinary, all the while retaining a quality of solid averageness that invites popular trust," it said.
It mused how apt it seemed to exhibit Kohl's XXL (extra extra large) size cardigan in the Museum of History in Bonn.
France and Belgium hailed Kohl for his efforts to achieve European unity, while a more Euro-sceptic Britain congratulated him on his 14-year term carefully avoiding the word "Europe".

Ex-European commission president Jacques Delors described Kohl as a "man of vision" on French radio and urged France, gripped by gloom over budget cuts and record unemployment, not to develop an inferiority complex about its enlarged neighbour.

Commentators were divided over whether Kohl had been right to overrule the Bundesbank and exchange firm West German marks for East German marks at a rate of one to one to achieve his goal of German unity as quickly as possible.
Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene said it was one of his greatest achievements, the Economist commented it was politically expedient, but the New York Time cast doubts.

"(Kohl's) decision to cushion the pain of reunification with unparalleled financial largess has produced at best mixed results from the staggering $600 billion in subsidies, incentives and aid that has poured into the former East Germany in the last six years," the New York Times said.

An Israeli official said Kohl was regarded as a "real friend of Israel". The official, who asked not to be identified, said the chancellor had forged a particularly warm relationship with Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin before his assassination.
